headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.9372). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 21 studies yielded an effect size of 1.02 (95% CI: 0.96–1.09), indicating no statistically significant association between polyunsaturated fat (pufa) and prostate cancer\aggressive. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 80.78%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

cases.excerpt: We tested this hypothesis in a prospective case-control study of 476 PCa cases and matched control subjects nested in the Physicians’ Health Study. The previously reported associations between fatty acids and PCa in this cohort were dramatically stronger among men diagnosed 10 or more years after blood collection.

comparison.excerpt: the relative risks per interquartile range

confidence_interval.excerpt: Among men diagnosed fewer than 10 years since blood collection, the relative risks per interquartile range were 1.03 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.86 to 1.25) for total mono-unsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) and 0.95 (95% CI = 0.78 to 1.15) for total poly-unsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) whereas among men diagnosed 10 or more years after blood draw the relative risks per interquartile range were 1.69 (95% CI = 1.21 to 2.34) for MUFA (Pheterogeneity = .01) and 0.59 (95% CI = 0.42 to 0.83) for PUFA (Pheterogeneity = .02).

cases.excerpt: During follow-up, we documented 4,308 incident cases of PCa, of whom 392 died from PCa.

comparison.excerpt: higher dietary total fat, SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs, and trans-fat acids intake were not associated with the incidence of PCa, with the HRs Q4vs.Q1 (95%CIs) for overall PCa incidence being 1.09 (0.93–1.28), 0.95 (0.82–1.10), 1.03 (0.92–1.15), 1.12 (0.98–1.27), and 0.95 (0.86–1.06), respectively
comparison.location: Results, Association between specific sources of fat and PCa incidence, paragraph 1

confidence_interval.excerpt: As Supplementary Table S7 shows, after full adjustment for potential confounders including demographic characteristics and key dietary nutrients (model 3), higher dietary total fat, SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs, and trans-fat acids intake were not associated with the incidence of PCa, with the HRs Q4vs.Q1 (95%CIs) for overall PCa incidence being 1.09 (0.93–1.28), 0.95 (0.82–1.10), 1.03 (0.92–1.15), 1.12 (0.98–1.27), and 0.95 (0.86–1.06), respectively (all P for trend >0.05). Intriguingly, when considering fat and fatty acid sources, we observed a positive association of total fat from dairy with the incidence of PCa (full adjusted HR Q4vs.Q1 : 1.13; 95% CI: 1.02–1.25; P for trend = 0.069), and association similar to PCa incidence was observed between SFAs from dairy intake (full adjusted HR Q4vs.Q1 : 1.12; 95% CI: 1.01–1.25; P for trend = 0.059) in the Table 2 .
confidence_interval.location: Results, Association between specific sources of fat and PCa incidence, paragraph 1

effect_size.excerpt: Intriguingly, when considering fat and fatty acid sources, we observed a positive association of total fat from dairy with the incidence of PCa (full adjusted HR Q4vs.Q1 : 1.13; 95% CI: 1.02–1.25; P for trend = 0.069), and association similar to PCa incidence was observed between SFAs from dairy intake (full adjusted HR Q4vs.Q1 : 1.12; 95% CI: 1.01–1.25; P for trend = 0.059) in the Table 2 . By using the restricted cubic spline regression, there was no evidence for non-linear associations of dietary SFAs from dairy or total fat from dairy intake with the incidence of PCa (all P non-linearity >0.05; Figure 2 ).
